---
title: "Pixel X and zebra stripes: the loop variable works harder"
---

![An X made of yellow and lime squares, like giant pixels: one diagonal runs from the top left down to the bottom right, the other from the bottom left up to the top right.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rstropek/ts-web-playground/main/exercises/0050-Loops/pixel-x.png){width=400}

The grid gave you a finished loop to copy, and the rays came with a
scaffold. This chapter takes the training wheels off: two exercises,
two empty canvases, and you write every loop yourself. Both drawings
look simple, and both hide a new skill. The pixel X teaches you to
*compute* with the loop variable, so that one variable places two
squares in one round. The zebra stripes teach you a second style of
loop, where the variable counts rounds instead of measuring pixels,
and where an `if` inside the loop body lets every second round act
differently.

## AI tutor {#sec-tutor-pixel-x}

Writing a loop from scratch is different from completing one. If your
diagonal bends the wrong way or your stripes are all one color, show
the tutor your loop and your loop table; the mistake is usually
visible in the table.

{{< tutor tutor-loops >}}

## Computing with the loop variable {#sec-mirror}

Start with the first diagonal of the X. A square sits at every
position where x and y are equal, so one `rect` with the loop
variable in both slots draws the whole diagonal:

```typescript
rect(i, i, GRID, GRID);
```

The second diagonal is the mirror image: when the yellow square is
near the top, the lime square is near the bottom. Mirroring a
position means subtracting it from the canvas height, roughly
`height - i`. But remember how `rect` measures: its first two
arguments are the *top left corner* of the rectangle. So `height - i`
would put the square's top edge where its bottom edge belongs, one
cell too low.
The correct top edge sits one grid step higher:

```typescript
rect(i, height - GRID - i, GRID, GRID);
```

One loop, one variable, and each round places a yellow square at
`(i, i)` and a lime square at `(i, height - GRID - i)`. The loop
variable is no longer just a position you draw at; it is a value you
compute with.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Test expressions at the edges
Before you trust an expression like `height - GRID - i`, feed it the
first and the last value of the loop on paper. First round,
`i = 25`, height 425: the lime square lands at y = 375, one cell
above the bottom edge. Last round, `i = 375`: y = 25, one cell below
the top edge. Both ends look right, so the middle will be right too.
Two small calculations catch most mirror mistakes.
:::

## Your exercise: Pixel X {#sec-pixel-x-exercise}

The canvas is 425 pixels, the squares are 25, and the X keeps a
margin of one empty cell on every side. The starter code contains
only the canvas setup and `noStroke()`.

1. **Paper first.** The canvas is 17 cells of 25 pixels. Sketch it,
   shade the diagonal squares, and read off: the first square sits at
   (25, 25), the last at (375, 375). Your loop runs from `GRID` while
   `i < SIZE - GRID`, both margins included in the plan.
2. **Draw the yellow diagonal alone.** Four steps, one `rect(i, i,
   GRID, GRID)` in the body, `fill("yellow")` before it. Run.
3. **Derive the lime expression on paper**, as in the section above,
   then add `fill("lime")` and the mirrored `rect` to the same loop
   body. Like the rays, the body switches colors every round: fill,
   yellow square, fill, lime square.
4. **Check the crossing.** In the middle of the X, the two diagonals
   meet. Which color wins there, and why? Think about the order of
   the two `rect` calls in your body.

{{< example https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rstropek/ts-web-playground/main/exercises/0050-Loops/pixel-x.yaml title="Pixel X" >}}

## Counting instead of measuring {#sec-counter}

![Eight horizontal stripes filling the canvas, alternating lime and yellow from top to bottom.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rstropek/ts-web-playground/main/exercises/0050-Loops/zebra-stripes.png){width=400}

All your loops so far measured pixels: `i` was an x or y coordinate,
and the update jumped one grid step. For the zebra stripes, a second
style is more natural: let the variable simply count the stripes,
0, 1, 2, 3, and compute the position from the count when you need
it. Stripe number `i` starts at `y = i * STRIPE_THICKNESS`:

```typescript
let i = 0;
while (i * STRIPE_THICKNESS < SIZE) {
    // draw stripe number i
    i += 1;
}
```

Both styles are correct, and you will use both. The measuring style
is direct: the variable *is* the position. The counting style keeps
the round number, and that is worth money here, because the stripe's
number decides its color.

Counting up by one is so common that TypeScript has an extra-short
form for it: `i++` does exactly what `i += 1` does. Until now the
course held the `++` back; from this chapter on you may use it, but
only for steps of one. For every other step size, `+=` stays the
right tool.

## A decision inside the loop {#sec-if-in-loop}

The loop body may contain any statements, including an `if`. Every
round can look at the loop variable and act differently:

```typescript
if (i % 2 === 0) {
    fill("lime");
} else {
    fill("yellow");
}
```

The test `i % 2 === 0` is the modulo operator in its parity role.
You used `% 2` in the binary chapter to split off the last binary
digit (@sec-extract-digits); the answer is 0 for even numbers and 1
for odd ones, even, odd, even, odd, in exactly the rhythm a zebra
needs. Stripes 0, 2, 4, and 6 come out lime, stripes 1, 3, 5, and 7
yellow.

## Your exercise: Zebra Stripes {#sec-zebra-exercise}

The canvas is 400 pixels, each stripe 50 thick, and the rule of the
exercise is strict: your output must match the goal picture exactly,
and you may use only a **single** while loop.

1. **Paper first.** 400 divided by 50 is eight stripes. Look closely
   at the goal picture: which color is the top stripe? Number the
   stripes 0 to 7 and write each one's color next to it.
2. **Make a loop table** with four columns: `i`, the stripe's y
   position `i * STRIPE_THICKNESS`, the value of `i % 2`, and the
   color.
3. **Write the loop**: the counting skeleton from above, the `if`
   deciding the fill, then one `rect` for stripe number `i`. It
   spans the full canvas width and is `STRIPE_THICKNESS` tall.
4. **Change the constants.** `STRIPE_THICKNESS = 25` must give 16
   thinner stripes, `STRIPE_THICKNESS = 100` four fat ones, with the
   colors still alternating from the same starting color.

{{< example https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rstropek/ts-web-playground/main/exercises/0050-Loops/zebra-stripes.yaml title="Zebra Stripes" >}}
